options: A bond formed when electrons are transferred from one atom to another
A bond formed when atoms share a pair of electrons
A bond that only happens between gases
questions.explanation: An ionic bond forms when electrons are transferred — one atom gives electrons, the other takes them.
questions.misconception: Sharing a pair of electrons is a COVALENT bond — the ionic bond is specifically about transferring electrons from one atom to another.

questions.prompt: In an ionic bond between sodium and chlorine, which atom gives the electron?
options: Sodium — the metal — gives it to chlorine, the nonmetal
Both atoms give one electron each
questions.explanation: Sodium, a metal with one lonely outer electron, gives it to chlorine, a nonmetal that needs one more to complete its shell.
questions.misconception: It is always the metal that gives and the nonmetal that takes — the metal's few outer electrons are easy to let go, while the nonmetal wants more to complete its shell.

questions.prompt: After sodium gives chlorine an electron, what holds the two atoms together?
options: The attraction between opposite charges — Na⁺ and Cl⁻
A physical hook between the atoms
questions.explanation: Sodium becomes positive Na⁺ and chlorine becomes negative Cl⁻, and opposite charges attract — that attraction IS the ionic bond.
questions.misconception: There is no shared pair and no physical hook — the bond is pure electrical attraction between the positive and negative ions.

questions.prompt: What structure do millions of sodium and chlorine ions form in table salt?
options: A repeating crystal lattice of alternating positive and negative ions
questions.explanation: Millions of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions lock into a repeating grid called a crystal lattice — the structure of table salt.
questions.misconception: Ionic compounds are not single molecules — they are giant repeating lattices where every ion is surrounded by ions of the opposite charge.
